newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti dents confidence in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti dents confidence in Italy.

text.p: The debacle surrounding Olivetti may have dented overseas investor confidence in Italy, but analysts said on Friday a string of new privatisation stocks coming to the Milan share market may help repair the damage.

Some large U.S. and European funds piled into Olivetti's massive rights issue late last year only to see their investment halved as the information technology group succumbed to internal management wrangling and a poor trading performance.
Clearly some big funds have had their fingers burnt by the plunge in Olivetti's fortunes, but analysts in Milan say investors must have known the risk of investing in the loss-making group.

With big share issues coming up, such as oil giant ENI next month and telecoms holding group STET early next year, analysts say international investors will be attracted to these well-managed groups and not put off by the problems at Olivetti.

Olivetti has not made a profit since 1990 and is regarded by many in Milan as the recovery story that never happened. Many funds were attracted by the potential of its 41.3 percent stake in fast-growing mobile phone operator Omnitel -- heavily highlighted in Olivetti's rights issue road show.

The rights issue was launched at 1,000 lire a share but Olivetti shares slipped to a record low of 465 lire a share earlier this week and the shares were at 540 lire at 1500 GMT, down 4.86 percent on the day.
"I can't believe that foreign investors were so blind not to know the problems of Olivetti, and they must have gone into Olivetti with their eyes open," said one Milan-based analyst.

But London-based analysts were not so certain. They pointed out that Olivetti was seen as a test case for Italian corporate governance and shareholder power, since some 70 percent of shareholders were from outside Italy.

Olivetti launched its massive 2.26 trilllion lire cash call late last year, giving foreign investors 70 percent of the company, but the trading performance failed to improve as chairman Carlo De Benedetti had promised and he bowed out.

Olivetti was ousted from the group in early September by his chief executive Francesco Caio. But then Caio followed this week after only 76 days at the helm when De Benedetti took revenge and put his own man Roberto Colannino in charge.
"The final deal in ousting Caio and bringing in a De Benedetti man has the fingerprints of De Benedetti and Mediobanca all over it," said one London-based analyst.

The deal to push out Caio was believed to have been organised by De Benedetti with the backing of secretive Milan merchant bank Mediobanca, which has influence in the boardrooms of most of Italy's top groups.

"International investors felt they were investing in a new Italy but they've seen that they have little power over the company, and the Italian market is still largely a closed club," said another London analyst.

Despite that Italy is making great strides towards a more developed stock market, incorporating European cross-border share trading rules, looking to privatise the Milan bourse and floating shares in well-established state-controlled groups such as ENI and STET. ($1=1524 lire)
